items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
items.summary: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: WebSockets for Beginners: Real-Time Data Without Refreshing
items.summary: WebSockets are how the web does real time. Chat apps, live scores, stock tickers, and multiplayer games all use them. The problem they solve is simple: normal HTTP means the browser asks and the server answers. WebSockets keep one connection open so the server can push new data the moment it exists — no refreshing, no polling. On the client, the API is tiny: const socket = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/live"); socket.onopen = () => { socket.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "join", room: "general" })); }; socket.onmessage = (event) => { const data = JSON.parse(event.data); console.log("New message:", data); }; On the server, Node.js with the ws library looks like this: import { WebSocketServer } from "ws"; const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 }); wss.on("connection", (socket) => { socket.on("message", (message) => { // Send the message to everyone connected wss.clients.forEach((client) => client.send(message.toString())); }); }); That is a working group chat in about fifteen lines. items.title: Untagged SD H.264 came out washed out after a WebCodecs re-encode: BT.601, BT.709 and visibleRect
items.summary: This article was drafted by an AI agent from my own code and test logs. Every number and code sample was checked against them. I've been re-encoding video to H.264 entirely in the browser with WebCodecs. Old AVI files with SD H.264 came out slightly washed out. Here is what was going on, and the small fix. Test clip: 5 seconds, 320×240, made with ffmpeg's testsrc, with no colour tags. After decoding with VideoDecoder in Chromium and re-encoding to H.264 in an MP4, the PSNR against the source was 24.5 dB (ffmpeg's psnr filter). Visually: colours a bit off, like a BT.601/BT.709 mix-up. Logging frame.colorSpace and the frame size showed two things for untagged SD H.264 in Chromium: colorSpace.matrix was bt709. By convention, untagged SD video is BT.601. The frame came back at a padded coded size: 320×258 for a 320×240 video. The real picture is in frame.visibleRect. Passing those frames straight to the encoder kept the BT.709 tag and the padding. items.title: What's Actually Inside an Enshrouded Save File (.ksd)
items.summary: Enshrouded keeps each character in a single .ksd file. Level, skill points, inventory, position, unlocked recipes — everything the game knows about that character lives in there. On Windows, saves sit under %USERPROFILE%\Saved Games\Enshrouded\, one folder per save slot. Copying that folder is the cheapest insurance in PC gaming: it costs nothing, and it is the only thing that saves you when a patch or a mod goes wrong. Most save tools ask you to install something, and a few ask you to upload your save to a server. Neither is necessary: a save file is small, and reading it is a client-side job — parse the file, show the fields, write back only what changed. I built one that works that way: Enshrouded Save Editor. It runs entirely in the browser, keeps the file on your machine, and needs no account. The same site documents where the saves live and how to back them up, which is honestly the part people need first. Back up the save folder before touching anything. Change one thing at a time, then load the game and check it. Keep the original file around until you are sure the edit is safe. Nothing exotic here — a small file, a parser, and a backup.

items.title: Turborepo for Beginners: Monorepos Without the Headache
items.summary: Turborepo is a build tool for JavaScript monorepos — projects where several apps and packages live in one repository. If you have a website, a docs site, and a shared component library in one repo, Turborepo makes building and testing them fast by only rebuilding what actually changed. A typical setup has a turbo.json at the root that describes your tasks: { "$schema": "https://turbo.build/schema.json", "tasks": { "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**"] }, "dev": { "cache": false, "persistent": true } } } The ^build part is the key idea: a package builds after its dependencies build. Turborepo figures out the order for you, so you never build things in the wrong sequence. The speed comes from caching. Run turbo run build once, and Turborepo remembers the result. Change one file in one package, run it again, and only the affected packages rebuild. On a team, remote caching means your teammate's build can be reused on your machine: npx turbo run build --filter=web The --filter flag builds just one app. That is how large teams keep CI fast even as the repo grows. Who is it for? Teams and solo developers with more than one package in a repo — a web app plus a mobile

items.title: Stop the agent from introducing a second state-management library when the repo already has one

The new dependency is a second source of truth, a second devtools path, and a new pattern for the next agent to copy. I’ve started treating a new state library in a feature PR as a scope break, even if the modal works. One widget is not a reason to change how the app holds state. Many training examples reach for Zustand or Redux Toolkit as the default. The model will not audit package.json unless you say “we already have X; do not add Y.” A modal’s open flag also does not need a store at all. You pay twice: bundle size, and a review surface where some flows go through the existing store and others go through the new one. items.title: Recoil for Beginners: Simple State Management for React
items.summary: Recoil is a state management library for React made by Facebook. It solves a specific problem: sharing state between components without prop drilling and without the boilerplate of Redux. If you have ever passed props through four components just to reach one button, Recoil is worth learning. The two core ideas are atoms and selectors. An atom is a single piece of state: import { atom, useRecoilState } from "recoil"; const countState = atom({ key: "countState", default: 0, }); function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useRecoilState(countState); return setCount(count + 1)}>{count} ; } Any component can read or update that atom, no matter where it sits in the tree. You just wrap your app in RecoilRoot once: import { RecoilRoot } from "recoil"; Selectors are derived state — values computed from atoms, like a filtered list: import { selector, useRecoilValue } from "recoil"; const doubledState = selector({ key: "doubledState", get: ({ get }) => get(countState) * 2, }); const doubled = useRecoilValue(doubledState); Only components that use a particular atom re-render when it changes. Install the package and wrap your app in the provider: npm install @chakra-ui/react @emotion/react import { ChakraProvider, Button, Stack } from "@chakra-ui/react"; function App() { return ( Save changes Cancel ); } That is already a working UI. Is it even worth outsourcing 2D character and environment art at this stage, or should I just push through and do it myself? items.title: The .npmignore trap: why npm publish ships files your .gitignore hides
items.summary: Adding a .npmignore makes npm stop reading .gitignore — so .env files, source maps, and build leftovers end up in the tarball. Git secret scanning never sees them. Originally published on ReleaseShield. .npmignore replaces .gitignore, it doesn't extend it With no .npmignore, npm uses your .gitignore to decide what to leave out. The moment you add a .npmignore (usually to drop src/ or test/), npm stops reading .gitignore for that directory. Everything git was hiding is back in scope. # .gitignore node_modules .env dist/*.map coverage/ # .npmignore (added later "to make the package smaller") src/ test/ # result: .env, dist/*.map and coverage/ are now in the tarball npm pack and npm publish read files from disk. Gitignored files exist on disk: the .env on your laptop, the source maps your bundler just wrote to dist/, the coverage report from the test step that ran before publish in CI. None of them were ever committed, so push protection, gitleaks, or any scanner that walks git history has nothing to look at. The tarball is a separate artifact and nobody inspects it. items.title: Renewal Alerts: User Queue Retries, Dead-Letter Consumers, and Email Webhooks
items.summary: Short answer: use a durable queue with a visible scheduled time, bounded retries, and a dead-letter state; make the consumer idempotent before choosing a queue product. For a renewal reminder that must wait until a business deadline, a database-backed schedule is usually the cheapest correctness anchor, while a managed broker is useful when delivery latency and throughput matter more than operational simplicity. The job sounds small: send an email or webhook when an account reaches its renewal window. The failure modes are not small. A worker can crash after the provider accepts a message, a webhook endpoint can return HTTP 429, or a customer can move the deadline while a message is already in flight. I care about revenue per hour, so I want the system to spend complexity only where a missed reminder would cost more than the engineer maintaining it. items.title: Stop Expecting the AI to Remember You - Build Chat Memory in Express for Beginners
items.summary: So you've used ChatGPT. You told it your name. Three messages later it still knows your name. So you think the model remembers you. 🥰 Then you build your first AI feature. You call the API with the user's new message. The user says "My name is Tolu". Next message: "What is my name?" The AI: "I don't know your name." 😭😭 You check your code. You check the API key. You blame the model. You blame your network provider. It was you. It was always you 😅 Here's the thing most people (including many developers) don't know: the model (the actual AI behind apps like ChatGPT) doesn't remember anything between requests. Every chat app you've used is quietly sending the whole conversation back to the model on every single message. Today we'll build that ourselves in Express and TypeScript: a forgetful chat route (the bug), one that remembers by resending the history, and one that trims the history so long chats don't blow up. items.title: React UseMemo Hook..
items.summary: useMemo is a React hook used to remember the result of a calculation between renders. Normally, whenever a component renders again, calculations inside the component are performed again. If a calculation is expensive, repeating it unnecessarily can affect performance. useMemo helps avoid repeating that calculation when its dependencies have not changed. Expensive calculations. Filtering or sorting large arrays. Calculating derived values from state or props. Avoiding unnecessary recalculations. Syntax: import { useMemo } from "react"; const result = useMemo(() => { return calculation; }, [dependencies]); Part Meaning useMemo React hook that remembers a calculation result. () => {} The function that performs the calculation. return Returns the calculated value. [dependencies] Values that determine when the calculation runs again.

items.title: Make Node exit on an unhandled rejection when Sentry is installed
items.summary: I assumed that adding Sentry to a Node service wouldn't change how it crashes. An unhandled rejection kills a plain Node process, so it should kill mine too. It doesn't. I tested it, and the service kept answering requests after the rejection. Sentry had the error, but the process never died, so nothing would have restarted it. TL;DR On Node 24 with no Sentry, an unhandled rejection kills the process with exit code 1. With @sentry/node 11.16.0 and a plain Sentry.init, the same rejection is reported at level error and the process keeps serving requests. Sentry.onUnhandledRejectionIntegration({ mode: 'strict' }) brings the crash back. The event is still delivered, at level fatal, and the exit code is 1. Any process.on('uncaughtException') or process.on('unhandledRejection') handler you add yourself keeps the process alive too, even with Sentry installed. I wanted to know exactly what Sentry changes about crashes, so I ran eight setups and then the fix, each in its own process. Versions, from run-0-versions.txt: v24.22.1 11.21.1 @sentry/node 11.16.0 Two pieces. items.title: Why Stripe sends your webhook twice (and how to process it once)
items.summary: Stripe will send you the same event twice. Your endpoint timed out. You returned a 5xx. The process died after the work but before the 200. In live mode, Stripe retries for up to three days, with exponential backoff. In a sandbox, it retries three times over a few hours. Stripe does not promise a single delivery, or a tidy order. The second POST is not a bug in Stripe. It is the contract. The unique key for a delivery is event.id. Store it atomically before you grant anything. The second delivery should return 200 and do nothing. A flag you read and then write is not enough. Two requests can both think they are first. A unique constraint, or a SET key NX lease, is what stops a double license. Return 200 for a duplicate. A 500 makes Stripe retry a delivery you already handled. Deduping only on event.id is necessary, and not sufficient. Creating a subscription can produce customer.subscription.created, invoice.created, invoice.paid, and charge.created. A Checkout payment can arrive as checkout.session.completed and later as checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded. Those are different Event objects. items.title: Interactive floor plan with hotspots in React
items.summary: Before: a PDF floor plan nobody zooms into. After: click a room, see the square footage. That is the whole pitch for an interactive floor plan, and it is one of the few animated elements on a real estate page that buyers actually use instead of just watching. The Hotspot image in Facade is the version I built after doing this for a new development client, and the approach works for any image that needs annotations: a floor plan, a site map, a kitchen render, a product photo. Here is how it is put together. The mistake I made the first time was positioning hotspots in pixels. It looked right on my screen and drifted on every other one, because the image scaled and the markers did not. The fix is to store every hotspot position as a percentage of the image's width and height. A marker at x: 26, y: 34 sits 26 percent from the left and 34 percent from the top, no matter how wide the container is. The data shape is small: export interface Hotspot { id: string; x: number; // percent from the left, 0 to 100 y: number; // percent from the top, 0 to 100 title: string; text?: string; meta?: Array ; } Rendering is one absolutely positioned wrapper per hotspot with left: ${x}% and top: ${y}%,

items.title: Decouple Your Backend: How Message Queues Prevent System Crashes
items.summary: It is 2 AM. Your on-call alert triggers because your backend service is failing health checks and returning 504 Gateway Timeouts. You dig through the logs expecting a database deadlock or a memory leak. Instead, you find the root cause: a third-party email provider slowed down, causing your HTTP request handlers to stack up, exhaust the connection pool, and bring down the entire checkout flow. Your core application logic did not fail. Your API crashed because a non-critical downstream dependency took the main process down with it. This failure mode happens when systems rely on synchronous processing for operations that do not need to happen in real time. Introducing a message queue eliminates this tight coupling. items.title: How Tamagotchis got us hooked on digital pets
items.summary: If you were are a kid in the late 1990s, there's a near-100 percent chance you either had a Tamagotchi or knew someone who did. items.title: JWT vs Session: The JWT Logout Problem Explained
items.summary: The interview question sounds simple: "If JWTs are stateless, how do you log a user out?" The production answer starts with a distinction. JWT is a token format. It does not require stateless validation, and not every access token is a JWT. OAuth access tokens may be self-contained or opaque. Logout behavior depends on the token type, validation path, threat model, and acceptable revocation delay. A signed JWT is usually three base64url-encoded parts: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6ImF0K2p3dCJ9 . eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL2lkLmV4YW1wbGUuY29tIiwiYXVkIjoiYXBpIiwiZXhwIjoxNzkxMjQ0ODAwfQ . signature Signing protects integrity and authenticity. It does not normally encrypt the claims; clients and anyone holding the token can read them. A resource server can validate a self-contained access token locally by checking its signature and claims. Secure validation includes, at minimum: An allowlisted algorithm, not whichever algorithm the token requests A trusted signing key bound to the expected issuer Exact issuer validation Audience validation for the current API Expiration and, where applicable, not-before validation with limited clock skew Token-type and application-specific authorization checks

items.title: Multipart Image Upload, Part 2: Chunking the Image Locally
items.summary: Multipart Image Upload: A Practical Guide for Web, Mobile and Backend Before any HTTP request goes out, the client has to turn one file into a list of chunks. This is the most code-heavy part of the series, and the idea is small: one formula, and one operation, reading a range of bytes. A 5.5 MB image, with a chunk size of 1 MB (1,048,576 bytes): Part 1 = 1.0 MB (bytes 0 to 1 MB) Part 2 = 1.0 MB Part 3 = 1.0 MB Part 4 = 1.0 MB Part 5 = 1.0 MB Part 6 = 0.5 MB (the remainder) The part count comes from: totalParts = ceil(fileSize / chunkSize) Here that's ceil(5.5 / 1) = 6. The last part is smaller whenever the file size isn't an exact multiple of the chunk size. That's normal, and the server has to accept it. The byte range for any part follows from the part number (1-based): start = (partNumber - 1) * chunkSize end = min(start + chunkSize, fileSize) // exclusive For part 6, start is 5 MB and end is min(6 MB, 5.5 MB), so the chunk is 0.5 MB. items.summary: I started building DocuPulse.AI with a fairly simple idea: many everyday document tasks are small, but the process of completing them is often more complicated than it needs to be. Sometimes I just need to compress a PDF before sending it. Another time I may need to merge a few PDF files, resize an image, convert a document, extract text from a PDF, or generate a QR code. These are not complicated goals from a user's point of view. But while building the tools behind them, I learned that making a file-processing workflow feel simple to the user requires a lot of work behind the scenes. This is the story of what I have learned while building DocuPulse.AI, a real ASP.NET Core project focused on practical PDF, image and document tools. I work with computers, documents, printers, systems and everyday IT problems regularly. One thing I noticed is how often a very small document task interrupts the actual work. items.title: Turning raw iPhone and Mac screen recordings into 1080p app demos offline
items.summary: Recording a 15-second screen clip of a new iPhone or Mac feature is fast. Turning that raw .mov into something clean enough for a changelog or social post usually takes much longer: trimming the Control Center pull-down at the end, cutting out a four-second loading pause, and zooming into the small button you tapped so phone viewers can actually read it. I built TapZoom to do that cleanup on a single screen, running natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac without uploading footage to a cloud editor. On iOS, app sandboxing prevents one app from reading raw touch coordinates recorded inside another app. Instead of pretending to capture hidden system touches, TapZoom runs a fast on-device frame-difference pass over the video (ignoring the top status bar clock) and places visual Screen Change Cues along the timeline wherever the UI updates. You can jump straight from cue to cue, step frame by frame, and tap directly on the preview canvas to drop a zoom highlight (Snappy, Smooth, or Gentle) and a high-contrast tap ripple. The first ten Google results are generic privacy-policy SaaS tools — Termly, iubenda, TermsFeed, Get Terms, plus a long tail of free templates. Most of them weren't built with App Review in mind. Not because the legal content is wrong. It's usually fine. The gap is that your privacy policy has to agree with three other things — your Info.plist permission strings, your App Privacy Details questionnaire in App Store Connect, and your PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file — and a generic generator has no idea what any of those say. So your policy ends up declaring data practices that don't match what your app actually does. This post is what an iOS privacy policy actually has to do, why generic generators miss the mark, and what to look for in a generator that's specifically built for App Store submission. If you're working through your full submission, see the broader checklist of every URL and file Apple requires for an iOS App Store submission. items.summary: You uploaded a build to App Store Connect. The processing-complete email arrives. You open it expecting a green check, and instead you see: ITMS-91053: Missing API declaration — Your app's code in the "YourApp" file references one or more APIs that require reasons, including the following API categories: NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults. items.title: After three App Store rejections, I built a pre-submit gate. Here is every check, and the bug behind each one
items.summary: Last week I wrote about three App Review rejections in one week: an ATT prompt the reviewer never saw, a China publishing-license request, and an ITMS-91064 privacy-manifest error. The week did not stop there. One app then got a 4.3(a), I pulled a build out of the review queue myself, and my own testing showed a tool that "didn't work" when it actually did. I'm one developer shipping three iOS apps (a prayer-times app in Flutter, a PDF password remover and an expense tracker in SwiftUI). Every rejection costs me a 24–48 hour cycle, so I turned each one into a line in a file called PRE-SUBMIT-GATE.md. Nothing gets submitted until every line has evidence next to it: a commit, a screenshot, or an API read-back. This post walks through the checks and the real bug behind each one. items.title: Triage flow for Xcode 16 and Swift 6 concurrency errors without leaving the IDE
items.summary: Swift 6 concurrency errors are the most expensive English text a macOS developer reads. A single MainActor isolation mistake can produce a wall of text spanning twenty lines, each a separate diagnostic with its own file and line reference. You copy it, lose a few lines to the wrapping, and now your clipboard holds an error message instead of the fragment you were about to paste. This is a triage flow for Xcode 16 / Swift 6 diagnostics that keeps you inside the IDE: read the root diagnostic first, work out which concurrency shape it is, then fix code. Isolation violation — mutation of captured var 'x' in concurrently-executing code. A captured value is mutated across actor boundaries; the note underneath names the isolation the closure requires. Sendable conformance — type 'Foo' does not conform to the 'Sendable' protocol. Something crosses an isolation domain while holding non-Sendable state. Global actor mismatch — main actor-isolated property 'y' can not be referenced from a nonisolated context. Typically a @MainActor type touched from a background task. items.title: Earth has a New Moon
items.summary: "Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN: Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. items.summary: A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. items.title: The most important number in AI (42 minute read)
items.summary: The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is a measure of AI progress developed by Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization. It is designed to be continuously updatable, and researchers can use it to look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models. This post covers how the ECI is constructed, the challenges of benchmark selection, whether it makes sense to talk about 'model IQ', whether static benchmarks stay relevant as models get better, and much more.

items.summary: The US Commerce Department is closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals to bypass export restrictions on advanced computer chips by renting access to them from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. items.title: World 2030 (8 minute read)
items.summary: Predicting how AI will affect the economy requires looking at all of the different components of that economy and figuring out how they might affect each other. items.title: OpenAI's ‘shepherds' affirm blockbuster physics result (3 minute read)
items.summary: Experts appointed by OpenAI have verified OpenAI's proof of the existence of the quantum Yang-Mills theory, a vital foundation for the Standard Model of particle physics. OpenAI created a committee to supervise the proof's release after backlash it received when it released a flood of more than 700 AI-generated proofs on a single day in October. This shepherding approach has riled some mathematicians, who see it as an act of needless gatekeeping. The experts do not claim to fully understand the proof yet, as it is too lengthy and complicated for human minds to immediately grasp.
